title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier and a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial generation that was evaluated under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation with ≤1 automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and the prespecified single‑draw conditioning the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We release preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts with the run bundle to support targeted follow‑up studies that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic properties—sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—determine operational safety and cannot be assured by surface syntactic checks alone. An operationally common solution is a generate→validate→repair scaffold that pairs a generative model with deterministic validators and constrained repair operators. Whether and how much such guarded pipelines increase the rate of unflagged, pre‑deployment passes depends critically on what is held fixed during evaluation (the estimand), the single‑draw quality of the generator, the validator's semantic coverage, and the permitted repair budget. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates the deterministic rescue from a verifier+bounded repair stage by conditioning on a single shared LLM draw per intent and allowing at most one automated repair. The primary research question is: does adding a deterministic verifier plus up to one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?
sections.related_work: Recent work documents a rapid proliferation of LLM applications to NetOps including intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated testing; several surveys and system papers examine tool‑augmentation patterns that enable LLMs to call external validators, planners, or simulators to coordinate multi‑step workflows. Prior empirical reports indicate that generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve surface correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but the magnitude depends on validator expressiveness, task distribution, and whether evaluations conflate validation benefits with resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration. Other literature addresses hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets (entropy/semantic detectors, retrieval mechanisms, self‑reflection) and hybrid repair methods that combine symbolic fault localization with generative repair. These threads motivate our design decisions: (1) clearly define the estimand to separate deterministic rescue from resampling effects; (2) use semantic validators that check sequencing and state invariants; and (3) make repair budget explicit so results map to operational policies.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) and fixed the primary estimand as the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) computed on N = 300 paired intents after applying inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration and analysis executor were archived prior to observing main‑run outcomes. Task generation and stratification. Tasks were produced deterministically by the registered task generator into a synthetic topology suite stratified into three difficulty strata (low/medium/high) and sampled 100 pairs per stratum for the confirmatory run. Each task encodes: the natural‑language intent, initial and expected final device states, sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), preservation invariants, and protected interfaces. Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic validator/repair rescue from generator resampling, we implemented a shared_initial estimand: for each pair the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate (single LLM draw) reused verbatim for both baseline and guarded conditions. The declared generator for shared_initial production was gpt-5-mini. Validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic validator implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule that checks sequencing invariants, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants expressed in the synthetic suite, and forbidden‑template protections. Scoring is binary: an unflagged candidate is a pass. The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair attempt (repair budget ≤ 1). The repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing and insertion edits; repairs are applied only if the validator flags the shared_initial candidate and are re‑validated deterministically. Contamination controls and missingness rules. We included deterministic contamination detection (negative controls and invariant checks) and prespecified that a pair would be excluded only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage. The optional preregistration pilot for discordance estimation was not executed before the main run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed. Execution accounting constraints. The executor enforced the single shared_initial draw per pair and repair budget ≤ 1 and recorded provider audit metadata and stage counts to enable deterministic reconciliation.
sections.results: Execution integrity. The confirmatory adapter completed the run with completed_episode_count = 600, yielding complete_pair_count = 300 paired observations under the shared_initial protocol and model_calls_used = 301 (one repair invocation observed). Deterministic reconciliation verified episode accounting and reported consistent stage counts with a single repair stage invoked across all pairs. Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline = 299/300 = 0.9966667; guarded = 300/300 = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. An exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts returned p = 1.0. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval computed with seed = 1729 and B = 10000 is [0.00, 0.01]. Per‑stratum diagnostics. Per the preregistered stratification the per‑stratum tallies were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. Thus the single discordant pair arose in the high (hard) stratum. Repair diagnostic. The solitary discordant pair invoked the permitted automated repair; validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission (missing explicit 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair performed one localized insertion of the missing sequencing command and the validator then reported valid == true for the corrected candidate. Cost and operational footprint. The guarded pipeline required one additional repair stage call across 300 pairs, indicating a minimal marginal model‑call cost under the chosen repair budget and operator design.
sections.discussion: Interpretation under shared_initial conditioning. The shared_initial estimand conditions on exactly one LLM draw per intent and thus measures only deterministic rescue attributable to a validator+bounded repair applied to the same candidate. This estimand maps to operational policies that tightly limit model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons. Under this conditioning and the supplied synthetic suite the baseline single‑shot generator produced near‑ceiling performance (299/300), so observable deterministic rescue was necessarily small in absolute terms. Implications for pipeline design. If operational policies permit resampling, verifier‑guided regeneration, or interactive steering, evaluations should change the estimand accordingly because such policies exploit generator variance and typically yield higher success rates. Conversely, when model calls are tightly budgeted, the shared_initial evaluation provides an operationally meaningful upper bound for deterministic post‑hoc rescue without resampling. Limitation driven insights. The observed rescue was a localized sequencing correction; other failure modes (reachability violations, forbidden ACL removal) were not observed at scale in this synthetic suite. Validator expressiveness (what properties can be checked) and repair operator richness are therefore primary determinants of a guarded pipeline's practical value. Practical guidance. Organizations must align evaluation estimands with deployment policies: choose shared_initial for single‑draw, low‑call budgets, or allow resampling/interactive workflows when multiple calls are affordable and tolerated by governance.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic validator+repair rescued a single sequencing omission under the bounded repair budget. The near‑ceiling baseline constrains inferential sensitivity to small absolute improvements under the selected estimand. We publish full preregistration, execution traces, validator diagnostics, and analysis artifacts so follow‑on studies can vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget and thereby measure broader operational tradeoffs.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically by the registered task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase guarded‑pipeline utility.
Single model and validator: evaluation used gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 only; results may not generalize to other LLM families or to richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing minimal discordance and limiting power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered optional pilot for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run before the main confirmatory execution.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one constrained automated repair; iterative or more permissive repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
